chapter: Producing, state of New Orleans music
title: Improving the New Orleans entertainment scene
summary: He urges sharper acts and more theatrics, comparing New Orleans to New York.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Almost finished. Are there any specific things you'd like to see done in New Orleans to encourage artists, either commercially or to have more confidence in themselves? Yes.

Sharpen up the acts. I do believe that, in spite of what New York has as downfall, and people talk about it, there are drama schools, there are good music schools, there are other good colleges. There's quite a bit of learning you can do on the street there, too. But there's so many good schools, and there are plays that you can go and see. There's the Winter Garden. There's the whole Broadway element. That if a kid is serious about what he's doing, he can think that I can maybe be right down there on Broadway later on. Some of those that don't go to Broadway, at least could be at the warehouse. But have your criteria set pretty high, I think, like New York. I'm not saying that everyone have to be a drama school graduate, but that element of entertainment, since television has come in, entertainment is at a high level now. So I think we are in competition with the rest of the world, not James Alley or nothing like that. Sometimes New Orleans have a tendency to be a big fish in a mayonnaise jar. You know what I mean? Definitely. Whereas New York, when you wake up and walk out to New York, there's so much going on and so many limousines and limos passing you and the right kind of suits and dresses. And real business being done, you know you have to shape up. You'll even have to brush up on whatever you're saying, how you're going to talk. And it's that serious if you're going to really be serious about this business. Our music affords us to be sort of happy-go-lucky and hip here. We have to be very careful about that because that doesn't draw many times the masses of the world. It'll draw the masses of New Orleans sometimes. And a certain group there will come to spectate you, who come to see you sometime as an animal in a cage. And I don't mean derogatory, but they get that out of it rather than that special we saw on Johnny Mathis on Channel 12 the other night. That's the other. I do think we need a bit more theatrics here in New Orleans. The theater groups, I don't know what they're doing, but I know theater groups, if they do well, it raises the level of the art in the area. It might say if the sculptures do better, they would raise the level, but since that's a silent art and painting and sound, theater speaks out, sings out, take in. I think we need more theatrics in our acts here, in our musical concept when we get ready to entertain. By now, a man that gets on the stage, a woman that gets on the stage, a boy, a girl, and plays, should be able to play or don't get up. And there are books on how to learn how to play. And do you have anything good to say after you know how to play? Yes or no? Now, since you have all those things, entertain me. That's the part where New Orleans falls short of our entertainment. Sometimes we like to say because there's nowhere to entertain. If I am practicing to be a good pianist, I don't care where, if there's a place for me to play. I just cannot do any less than try and become good at this. I hope that in that, you got something of what I meant by what I think New Orleans could do to improve the musical scene, just to improve the entertainment scene because the universities, I'm sorry, are about to turn out some really good musicians. There's a good generation of musicians coming now.
